This is claim petition u/s 166/140 M.V. Act seeking compensation in respect of injuries suffered by the petitioner in a road side accident.

As per the facts on 19.11.2013 at about 6.30 pm petitioner Ramesh Kumar Doshi vs Devender Singh Etc on 12 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72404711/
1 was going from Noida to Delhi on his motorcycle no.DL-1SU-2024, at normal speed, complying traffic rules.

sentences.text: When petitioner stated to have reached near village Gaija, Noida, one Indica car no.DL-3CAX-6706 came at a very high speed and driving in a rash and negligent manner, hit the petitioner's vehicle due to which petitioner fell down and suffered grievous injuries.
It is stated that accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of driver/ respondent no.1 of offending vehicle no.DL-3CAX-6706.
In respect of accident FIR No.837/2013 was registered at PS Phase-II, Gautam Budh Nagar u/s 279/338/427 IPC.
Claim petition was filed against respondent no.2, owner and respondent no.3 being insurer of the offending vehicle.

2. WS was filed by respondent no.1 and 2 taking an objection that claim petition is not maintainable,
petitioner concealed material facts.
It is stated that even otherwise the vehicle no.DL-3CAX-6706 was duly insured and respondent no.1 was having valid DL.

3. Respondent no.3/insurance also filed WS taking an objection that claim petition is devoid of cause of action and respondent no.3 is liable for compensation only in case when there is no violation of terms and condition of insurance policy including valid DL, permit, RC, fitness certificate etc.
It is pleaded that respondent no.3 is entitled for all the legal pleas including reserve its right to take plea u/s 170 of M.V. Act.
Averments of the claim petition have been denied in totality.
4. On the basis of pleadings of the parties following issues were framed by ld.

sentences.text: It is settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

sentences.text: Petitioner has appeared in the witness box as PW1 and has testified the circumstances in which accident occurred.

PW1 states that on 19.11.2013 when he was going from Noida to Delhi on his motorcycle, when he reached near village Gaija, he was hit by offending vehicle no. DL-2CAX-6706 which was being driven in rash and negligent manner and he sustained grievous injuries.
PW1 was duly cross examined however nothing substantive came in the cross examination to disbelieve the version of PW1 regarding the accident.
Rather PW1 reiterated that at the time of accident he was on left side of the road and offending vehicle came from opposite direction at a very high speed and struck him.
PW1 specifically denied that he was driving his motorcycle at very high speed or that accident occurred due to his negligence.

Evidence of PW1 gets corroboration from criminal case documents, the certified copy of which is on the record as Ex.PW1/3, perusal of site plan prepared by the IO also indicate that accident occurred when respondent no.1 while driving vehicle no.DL-2CAX-6706 went towards the wrong side of the road and hit motorcycle of the injured.
Police report u/s 173 Cr.PC, mechanical inspection report and other documents also corroborate the version of PW1.

Consequently there is sufficient evidence on record to conclude that accident in question has occurred due to rash and negligent driving of respondent no.1 while driving offending vehicle no.DL-2CAX-6706.
Issue accordingly decided in favour of petitioner.

The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary Ramesh Kumar Doshi vs Devender Singh Etc on 12 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72404711/
3 damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

sentences.text: In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit upto the date of trial; (iii) other material loss.

So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned,
they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit;
(iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e. on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, discomfort,
disappointment, hardship, frustration and mental stress in life."
11. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
4.

The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation MACT No.908/2016 SHAILENDER SHAILENDER Page 5 MALIK Date: 2024.08.12 16:34:47 +0530 should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)

(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.

(iii) Future medical expenses.

Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
(iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage)
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii), (a) and (iv).

future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.

In the light of the aforementioned judgments, the compensation to which the petitioner is entitled shall be as under:-

(2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India determined the broad criteria for assessment of permanent disability for ascertaining the purpose of future loss of earning and also laid down step by step procedure for assessment of disability and for ascertainment to the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity.

But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.

sentences.text: Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood."
....If doctor has given evidence about percentage of permanent disability, Tribunal will have to seek MACT No.908/2016 SHAILENDER Page 9 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK
Date: 2024.08.12 16:35:13 +0530 doctors opinion as to whether it is possible to deduce the corresponding functional permanent disability with reference to whole body and if so to what percentage.

13. We may now summarize the principles discussed above:
(i). All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity.
(ii). The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.

To put it differently, the percentage of loss of earning capacity is not the same as the percentage of permanent disability (except in a few cases, where the Tribunal on the basis of evidence, concludes that percentage of loss of earning capacity is the same as percentage of permanent disability).

(iii). The doctor who treated an injured- claimant or who examined him subsequently to assess the extent of his permanent disability can give evidence only in regard the extent of permanent disability.
The loss of earning capacity is something that will have to be assessed by the Tribunal with reference to the evidence in entirety.

(iv). The same permanent disability may result in different percentages of loss of earning capacity in different persons, depending upon the nature of profession,
occupation or job, age, education and other factors."

17. Keeping in view the ratio as discussed above, in the present case it is evident on record that as a result of the injuries sustained by petitioner in an accident, he suffered 54% permanent disability in relation to right lower limb.

sentences.text: The disablement and loss of earning capacity are two different aspects and may not corresponding to each other and the loss of income has to be seen considering the profession in which the petitioner was engaged at the time of accident.
As per case of petitioner, he was working as field officer at the time of accident.
18. In Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar (supra) Hon'ble Apex Court in para 11 and 12 has observed that Tribunal should not be a silent spectator when medical evidence is tendered regarding injuries.

Tribunal is required to hold inquiry into the claim for determining just compensation by assessing the medical permanent disability as well as functional disability keeping in view nature of work,
profession etc. of the injured.
The percentage of permanent disability of whole body cannot be presumed to be percentage loss of earning.
Therefore Tribunal is bound to assess corresponding functional disability to compute the future loss of income.
19. Having considered the entire evidence, medical documents reflect that petitioner suffered grievous injuries and suffered 54% of permanent disability.

In such circumstances when petitioner has lost his livelihood as he used to work as field officer on account of his accidental injuries, this Tribunal is of considered view that the functional disability of the petitioner in relation to his job was half of the medical disability i.e. 27% of medical permanent disability.
For assessing the future prospects, petitioner would considered to be suffering from functional disability to the extent of 27%.
20. Further, law is well settled that there should be no departure from the multiplier method in injury cases also [refer: Sandeep Khanuja vs. Atul Dande & Anr., (2017) 3 SCC 351].

As such multiplier to be applied in the present case would be 16 as applicable to age group between 31-35 years, would be applicable as per settled principle laid down in case of Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121.

Moreover, the law has been well settled by the decisions of Supreme Court in the cases of Sandeep Khanuja (supra) and Erudhaya Priya vs.
State Express Transport Corporation Ltd. 2020 SCC OnLine SC 601, that while applying the multiplier method, future prospects on advancement in life and career are also to be taken into consideration.

25. In this case, as per medical documents proved on record, petitioner was found to have suffered grievous injuries on his right leg and lower part of chin.
The treatment record and bills/invoices of pharmacy further show that petitioner had been taking continuous treatment.

Thus, it is clear that petitioner must have suffered immense pain and suffering during his treatment and therefore, I am of the opinion that an amount of Rs.1,00,000/- would be just and fair compensation for pain,
sufferings and mental trauma suffered by the petitioner as consequences of injuries sustained in the accident.
Accordingly, Rs.1,00,000/- is granted to the petitioner under this head.

It is evident on record that even after completion of treatment, petitioner sustained 54% medical permanent physical disability in relation to right lower limb which has been assessed as 27%

It cannot be ignored that with the aforementioned disability, petitioner is bound to face difficulties throughout his life and will not be able to enjoy the amenities of life to the fullest.
In view of this, the petitioner is granted a compensation of Rs.50,000/- under this head.

SHAILENDER MALIK Page 2  MALIK Date: 2024.08.12  16:34:23 +0530 (1)Whether respondent no.1 was driving car bearing no.DL- 2CAX-6706 on 19.11.2013 at 6.30 am near Village Gajja, Noida in a high speed and in a rash and negligent manner and hit against motorcycle no.DL-1SU-2024 being driven by petitioner as a result petitioner fell down and sustained injuries?
OPP (2)Whether the petitioner is entitled for any compensation, if so and for what amount?
Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide whether there is any permanent disability and if so, the extent of such permanent disability.
Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood."

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v.
Sakshi Bhutani & Others.
Bimla Devi & Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
9.
The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.
The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation MACT No.908/2016 SHAILENDER SHAILENDER Page 5 MALIK Date: 2024.08.12 16:34:47 +0530 should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
In such circumstances since it has come in the facts that accident has occurred within the jurisdiction of Gautam Budh Nagar, UP, petitioner is entitled for minimum wages of unskilled worker of UP at the time of accident which is Rs.5,200/- per month.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.
(ii). The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.
The disablement and loss of earning capacity are two different aspects and may not corresponding to each other and the loss of income has to be seen considering the profession in which the petitioner was engaged at the time of accident.
As per case of petitioner, he was working as field officer at the time of accident.
18. In Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar (supra) Hon'ble Apex Court in para 11 and 12 has observed that Tribunal should not be a silent spectator when medical evidence is tendered regarding injuries.
Tribunal is required to hold inquiry into the claim for determining just compensation by assessing the medical permanent disability as well as functional disability keeping in view nature of work,
profession etc. of the injured.
The percentage of permanent disability of whole body cannot be presumed to be percentage loss of earning.
Therefore Tribunal is bound to assess corresponding functional disability to compute the future loss of income.
19. Having considered the entire evidence, medical documents reflect that petitioner suffered grievous injuries and suffered 54% of permanent disability.
In such circumstances when petitioner has lost his livelihood as he used to work as field officer on account of his accidental injuries, this Tribunal is of considered view that the functional disability of the petitioner in relation to his job was half of the medical disability i.e. 27% of medical permanent disability.
For assessing the future prospects, petitioner would considered to be suffering from functional disability to the extent of 27%.
20. Further, law is well settled that there should be no departure from the multiplier method in injury cases also [refer: Sandeep Khanuja vs. Atul Dande & Anr., (2017) 3 SCC 351].
As such age of petitioner as on date of accident i.e. 19.11.2013 was 33 years.
Moreover, the law has been well settled by the decisions of Supreme Court in the cases of Sandeep Khanuja (supra) and Erudhaya Priya vs.
State Express Transport Corporation Ltd. 2020 SCC OnLine SC 601, that while applying the multiplier method, future prospects on advancement in life and career are also to be taken into consideration.
Thus, considering the petitioner was self employed and below the age of 40 years at the time of accident, an addition of income to the extent of 40% towards future prospects has to be counted.
Keeping in view the medical documents placed on record, this Tribunal is of the view that petitioner must have engaged the services of some attendant and he is required to be awarded compensation under this head for a period of three months.
Therefore petitioner in the opinion of this Tribunal is also entitled for minimum wages of unskilled worker in Delhi i.e. Rs.5,200 X 3 which comes out to be Rs.15,600/-.
Thus, it is clear that petitioner must have suffered immense pain and suffering during his treatment and therefore, I am of the opinion that an amount of Rs.1,00,000/- would be just and fair compensation for pain,
sufferings and mental trauma suffered by the petitioner as consequences of injuries sustained in the accident.
